_: The claims Knos can prove on NEAR testnet: each from a real paper (its words quoted from its abstract), with its locked test in near/agents/job/ and its two agents' code in near/agents/ (hyperloglog) or near/agents/solutions/. The test's sha256 is the criteria hash every job for the claim is opened with. Read by the site (scripts/site_pages.py) and the hosted server (apps/wanted/knos_wanted/near_live.py).

claims.name: hyperloglog
claims.plain: HyperLogLog counts 30,000 different visitors within 10% using at most 1.5 kilobytes of memory.
claims.paper: HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm
claims.quote: For instance, the new algorithm makes it possible to estimate cardinalities well beyond 10^9 with a typical accuracy of 2% while using a memory of only 1.5 kilobytes.
claims.locked: count 30,000 visitors within 10%, in at most 1.5 kilobytes
claims.question: Does HyperLogLog count 30,000 visitors within 10% using at most 1.5 kilobytes?
claims.not_checked: counts beyond 30,000 visitors, or the paper's 2% figure at a billion items
claims.outside_test: None found: the authors published no test code with the paper.

claims.name: jump-hash
claims.plain: Jump consistent hash moves only about 1 key in 11 when 10 buckets become 11, with nothing stored.
claims.paper: A Fast, Minimal Memory, Consistent Hash Algorithm
claims.quote: jump consistent hash requires no storage, is faster, and does a better job of evenly dividing the key space among the buckets and of evenly dividing the workload when the number of buckets changes.
claims.paper_number: no storage, an even split, and few keys moved when buckets change
claims.locked: place 100,000 keys in 10 buckets, then 11: between 8.2% and 10.0% move, all to the new bucket, the fullest bucket at most 5% over the mean, nothing stored
claims.question: Does jump consistent hash move only about 1 key in 11 when 10 buckets become 11?
claims.not_checked: bucket counts other than 10 and 11, or the paper's claim that it is faster
claims.outside_test: None found: the paper prints its algorithm as code, with no test suite.

claims.name: xor-filter
claims.plain: An xor filter answers set membership with under 0.5% false positives in at most 10 bits per key, where a Bloom filter of that size cannot.
claims.paper: Xor Filters: Faster and Smaller Than Bloom and Cuckoo Filters
claims.quote: We find that xor filters can be faster than Bloom and cuckoo filters while using less memory.
claims.paper_number: less memory than a Bloom filter for the same answers
claims.locked: hold 50,000 keys, miss none, say yes to under 0.5% of 200,000 others, in at most 10 bits per key
claims.question: Does an xor filter give under 0.5% false positives in at most 10 bits per key?
claims.not_checked: speed, which the paper also claims, or the smaller xor+ variant
claims.outside_test: The authors publish tests in C and Go for their own implementations (FastFilter/xor_singleheader at 5426b7d84994 and FastFilter/xorfilter at 3fd77f5b8c19, Apache-2.0); they cannot run unchanged against an agent's Python module, so they are not a second locked test.
claims.method: Graf and Lemire's xor filter: each key maps by three hashes to one slot in each third of a table of about 1.23 n + 32 one-byte slots; build by peeling (repeatedly take a slot that only one remaining key maps to, push that key with that slot), then assign in reverse order so each key's 8-bit fingerprint equals the xor of its three slots; if peeling stalls, retry with a new hash seed. Keep only the table (as bytes), the seed and the table size. For 50,000 keys it must build in a few seconds: keep the three positions of each key in flat lists of ints, count and xor per slot in lists, peel with one stack, and avoid sets, dicts and per-key objects.

claims.name: morris-counter
claims.plain: A Morris counter counts 100,000 events within 10% in a 12-bit register, where an exact count needs 17 bits.
claims.quote: Storing a counter incremented N times would naively consume O(log N) bits of memory. In 1978 Morris described the very first streaming algorithm: the "Morris Counter".
claims.paper_number: O(log log N) bits for an approximate count, against O(log N) for an exact one
claims.locked: count 100,000 events within 10% in at least 19 of 20 runs, in a register of at most 12 bits
claims.question: Does a Morris counter count 100,000 events within 10% in a 12-bit register?
claims.not_checked: the paper's own new algorithm or its lower bound: only the Morris counter it describes
claims.outside_test: None found: the paper is proofs, with no test code.
claims.method: Morris's counter with a base 1 + a: each event raises the register X by one with probability (1 + a) ** -X, and the count is ((1 + a) ** X - 1) / a. Base 2 (a = 1) is far too coarse for 10%; a small a, about 0.002, gives that accuracy while X for 100,000 events stays under 2 ** 12.

claims.name: kepler-10b
claims.plain: The planet Kepler-10b goes around its star once every 0.837495 days, found again in NASA's public Kepler light curve.
claims.locked: find the period in 4 years of Kepler light curve inside 0.837490 to 0.837499 days and within 3 sigma of NASA's DR25 value, in under 20 s
claims.question: Does Kepler-10b go around its star every 0.837495 days?
claims.not_checked: the planet's size, mass or transit depth: only its orbital period
claims.outside_test: None found: the paper publishes the ephemeris, not code.
claims.caveat: The 2011 paper used 8 months of data; this test uses all 4 public years, and the answer must still fall inside the 2011 interval.
claims.data_credit: NASA Kepler mission light curves of KIC 11904151 from MAST at STScI (public domain)

claims.name: landsat-8-orbit
claims.plain: Landsat 8's published orbit, 705 km up and tilted 98.2 degrees, is sun-synchronous: simulated with Earth's equatorial bulge, its orbit plane turns 0.98565 degrees a day.
claims.quote: Altitude: 705 km (438 mi) ... Inclination: 98.2 degrees ... Orbit: Near-polar, sun-synchronous ... Period of Revolution: 99 minutes; ~14.5 orbits/day
claims.paper_number: sun-synchronous: the orbit plane turns 360 degrees a tropical year, 0.98565 degrees a day, and one orbit takes 99 minutes
claims.locked: simulate the published orbit 5 days with Earth's J2 bulge: the plane turns within 1% of 0.98565 degrees a day, an orbit takes 99 minutes within 0.5, energy is kept, and a polar orbit does not turn, in under 18 s
claims.question: Does Landsat 8's orbit turn with the Sun, 0.98565 degrees a day?
claims.not_checked: Landsat 8's real tracking data: only a simulation from the published orbit
claims.outside_test: None found: NASA publishes the orbit, not code.
claims.caveat: The plus or minus 1% tolerance was set by Knos, because NASA publishes rounded values (98.2 degrees, 99 minutes).
claims.data_credit: NASA's Earth Fact Sheet (NSSDC) and NASA Goddard's Landsat 8 page (public domain)

claims.name: cmapss-engine-life
claims.plain: A plain Ridge regression predicts how many cycles NASA's simulated FD001 jet engines have left, off by 16.634 cycles RMS.
claims.paper: Remaining Useful Life Estimation for Turbofan Engines: A Comparative Study of Classical, CNN, and LSTM Approaches
claims.quote: Table III, Raw Ridge Regression, FD001: RMSE 16.634, MAE 13.570
claims.paper_number: RMSE 16.634 and MAE 13.570 cycles on the 100 FD001 test engines
claims.locked: Ridge regression trained on 80 of the 100 training engines: RMSE within 0.005 of 16.634 and MAE within 0.005 of 13.570, in under 20 s
claims.question: Does a Ridge baseline predict FD001 engine life with an RMSE of 16.634 cycles?
claims.not_checked: the paper's CNN and LSTM results, or any real engine: only its Ridge baseline on NASA's simulated engines
claims.outside_test: None found: the preprint publishes no code.
claims.caveat: The figure comes from a 2026 preprint that is not peer-reviewed.
claims.data_credit: NASA Ames Prognostics Center of Excellence, C-MAPSS turbofan data (Saxena and others, 2008)
